'''''Catalpa bignonioides''''' is a short-lived<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Gilman |first1=Edward F |last2=Watson |first2=Dennis G |last3=Klein |first3=Ryan W |last4=Koeser |first4=Andrew K |last5=Hilbert |first5=Deborah R |last6=McLean |first6=Drew C |title=ENH289/ST130: Catalpa spp.: Catalpa |url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/ST130 |website=Ask IFAS - Powered by EDIS |language=en-US |publication-date=December 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Southern Catalpa |url=https://woodstock.recdesk.com/RecDeskPortal/Portals/770/Southern%20Catalpa%20-%20Tree%20Facts.pdf |website=Arbor Day Foundation}}</ref> [[species]] of ''[[Catalpa]]'' that is [[native plant|native]] to the [[southeastern United States]] in [[Alabama]], [[Florida]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[Louisiana]], and [[Mississippi]]. Common names include '''southern catalpa''', '''cigartree''', and '''Indian bean tree'''<ref>{{GRIN | accessdate = 22 December 2017}}</ref><ref name = RHSPF/> It is commonly used as a garden and [[urban forestry#Street trees|street tree]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s12228-017-9471-7|title=Taxonomic revision of the genus Catalpa (Bignoniaceae) |year=2017 |last1=Olsen |first1=Richard T. |last2=Kirkbride |first2=Joseph H. |journal=Brittonia |volume=69 |issue=3 |pages=387–421 |bibcode=2017Britt..69..387O |s2cid=45922216 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Description==
{{singlesource|section|date=October 2023}}
''Catalpa bignonioides'' is a [[deciduous]] tree growing to {{convert|25|-|40|ft}} tall with an equal or greater spread,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-12-12 |title=Catalpa bignonioides |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=cabi8&__cf_chl_tk=NG8a6mfEOKKLbqZiNYzBq_vmrrgxDTMNI8PrEQG8b0o-1708844435-0.0-3922 |website=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center |publisher=The University of Texas at Austin}}</ref> with a trunk up to {{convert|1|m|0}} diameter, with brown to gray [[Bark (botany)|bark]], maturing into hard plates or ridges. The short thick trunk supports long and straggling branches which form a broad and irregular head.  The roots are fibrous and branches are brittle, its juices are watery and bitter tasting.<ref name=Keeler>{{cite book
  | last =Keeler
  | first =Harriet L.
  | title =Our Native Trees and How to Identify Them
  | url =https://archive.org/details/ournativetreesa02keelgoog
  | publisher =Charles Scribner's Sons
  | year =1900
  | location =New York
  | pages =225–228 }}</ref>

The leaves are large, bright green and heart shaped, being {{convert|20-30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|15-20|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} broad. They appear late, and as they are full-grown before the flower clusters open, they add much to the beauty of the blossoming tree. They secrete [[nectar]], a most unusual characteristic for leaves, by means of groups of tiny glands in the [[Leaf|axils]] of the primary veins.<ref name=Keeler /> The nectar secretion starts a week before the tree's flowers bloom and up to ten days after the blooming stops.<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://archive.org/details/sim_american-bee-journal_1938-07_78_7 |title=American Bee Journal  1938-07: Vol 78 Iss 7 |date=July 1938 |publisher=Dadant and Sons, Inc. |others=Internet Archive |language=English}}</ref>

[[Image:Catalpa bignonioides in Le Roeulx AR1cJPG.jpg|thumb|left|''C. bignonioides'' 'Aurea']]

The flowers are 2.5–4 cm across, trumpet shaped, white with yellow spots inside; they grow in [[panicle]]s of 20–40. In the northern states of the USA, it is a late bloomer, putting forth great panicles of white flowers in June or early in July when the flowers of other trees have mostly faded. These cover the tree so thickly as almost to conceal the full-grown leaves. The general effect of the flower cluster is a pure white, but the individual [[Corolla (botany)|corolla]] is spotted with purple and gold, and some of these spots are arranged in lines along a ridge, so as to lead directly to the nectar within. A single flower when fully expanded is {{convert|2|in|cm|abbr=on|round=5|order=flip}} long and {{convert|1+1/2|in|mm|round=5|order=flip|abbr=on}} wide. It is two-lipped and the lips are lobed, two lobes above and three below, as is not uncommon with such corollas. The flower is perfect, possessing both [[Stamen|stamens]] and [[pistils]]; nevertheless, the law of elimination is at work and of the five stamens that are expected to be found, three have aborted, ceased to bear [[Stamen|anthers]] and have become filaments simply. Then, too, the flowers refuse to be self-fertilized. Each flower has its own stamens and its own stigma but the lobes of the stigma remain closed until after the anthers have opened and discharged their pollen; after they have withered and become effete then the stigma opens and invites the wandering bee. The entire [[Caryophyllaceae|Pink family]] behave in this way.<ref name=Keeler />
[[File:Catalpa bignoioides 004.JPG|thumb|The fruit of the Southern Catalpa resembles bean pods.]]
[[File:Catalpa bignonioides MHNT.BOT.2023.13.40.jpg|thumb|''Catalpa bignonioides'' ([[MHNT]])]]

The [[fruit]] is a long, thin seed pod 20–40 cm long and 8–10 mm in diameter; it often stays attached to the tree during winter. The capsule contains numerous flat light brown seeds with two papery wings. Despite its appearance, it is not closely related to true [[beans]].

It is closely related to the Northern Catalpa (''[[Catalpa speciosa|C. speciosa]]''), and can be distinguished by the flowering [[Panicle|panicles]], which bear a larger number of smaller flowers, and the slightly slenderer seed capsules.

* Bark: Light brown tinged with red. Branchlets forking regularly by pairs, at first green, shaded with purple and slightly hairy, later gray or yellowish brown, finally reddish brown.  Contains [[tannin]].
* Wood: Light brown, [[Sapwood (wood)|sapwood]] nearly white; light, soft, coarse-grained and durable in contact with the soil.
* Winter buds: No terminal bud, uppermost bud is axillary.  Minute, globular, deep in the bark.  Outer scales fall when spring growth begins, inner scales enlarge with the growing shoot, become green, hairy and sometimes {{convert|2|in|mm|round=5|order=flip|abbr=on}} long.
* Leaves: Opposite, or in threes, simple, {{convert|6-10|in|mm|sigfig=2|order=flip|abbr=on}} long, four to five broad.  Broadly ovate, cordate at base, entire, sometimes wavy, acute or acuminate.  Feather-veined, midrib and primary veins prominent.  Clusters of dark glands, which secrete nectar are found in the axils of the primary veins.  They come out of the bud involute, purplish, when full grown are bright green, smooth above, pale green, and downy beneath.  When bruised they give a disagreeable odor.  They turn dark and fall after the first severe frost.  [[Petiole (botany)|Petioles]] stout, [[terete]], long.
* Flowers: June, July.  Perfect, white, borne in many-flowered thyrsoid panicles, {{convert|8-10|in|mm|sigfig=2|order=flip|abbr=on}} long.  [[Pedicel (botany)|Pedicels]] slender, downy.
* Calyx: Globular and pointed in the bud; finally splitting into two, broadly ovate, entire lobes, green or light purple.
* Corolla: Campanulate, tube swollen, slightly oblique, two-lipped, five-lobed, the two lobes above smaller than the three below, imbricate in bud; limb spreading, undulate, when fully expanded is {{convert|1+1/2|in|mm|round=5|order=flip|abbr=on}} wide and nearly {{convert|2|in|mm|round=5|order=flip|abbr=on}} long, white, marked on the inner surface with two rows of yellow blotches and in the throat on the lower lobes with purple spots.
* Stamens: Two, rarely four, inserted near the base of the corolla, introrse, slightly exserted; anthers oblong, two-celled, opening longitudinally; filaments flattened, thread-like.  Sterile filaments three, inserted near base of corolla, often rudimentary.
* Pistil: Ovary superior, two-celled; style long, thread-like, with a two-lipped stigma.  Ovules numerous.
* Fruit: Long slender capsule, nearly cylindrical, two-celled, partition at right angles to the valves.  {{convert|6-20|in|mm|round=50|order=flip|abbr=on}} long, brown; hangs on the tree all winter, splitting before it falls.  Seeds {{convert|1|in|mm|round=5|order=flip|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|1/4|in|mm|round=5|order=flip|abbr=on}} wide, silvery gray, winged on each side and ends of wings fringed.<ref name=Keeler />

==Induced defenses==
A 2003 study by J. Ness showed that when a hawkmoth caterpillar ''[[Ceratomia catalpae]]'' started eating the leaves of ''C. bignonoides'', the leaves produced extra nectar. The nectar in turn attracted a greater number of bodyguard ants ''[[Forelius pruinosus]]'' to the damaged leaves, thus giving added protection to the whole plant.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ness|first=J.|date=January 2003|title=Catalpa bignonioides alters extrafloral nectar production after herbivory and attracts ant bodyguards|journal=Oecologia|language=en|volume=134|issue=2|pages=210–218|doi=10.1007/s00442-002-1110-6|pmid=12647162|bibcode=2003Oecol.134..210N|s2cid=20232356|issn=0029-8549}}</ref> This is an example of a tree exhibiting a [[Symbiosis|symbiotic relationship]] with nearby insects.[[Image:Catalpa bignonioides Aurea JPG1a.jpg|thumb|''C. bignonioides'' 'Aurea']]

==Distribution==
In the USA, ''Catalpa bignonioides'' is undoubtedly a Southern tree. Europeans first observed the tree growing in the fields of the [[Cherokee]] Native American tribes. However, it can flourish in the North as well, and accordingly its original range is somewhat in doubt.<ref name=Keeler />

Despite its southern origins, it has been able to grow almost anywhere in the United States and southernmost Canada, and has become widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] outside its restricted native range.{{Citation needed|reason=is this true of C. bignonioides or is this about C. speciosa?|date=June 2011}}

==Cultivation and uses==
It is a fast-growing tree<ref>{{Cite book |last=Roth |first=Susan A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=g-vThywrFWIC&dq=%22Catalpa+bignonioides%22+%22fast%22&pg=PA61 |title=Taylor's Guide to Trees: The Definitive, Easy-to-use Guide to 200 of the Garden's Most Important Plants |date=2001 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt |isbn=978-0-618-06889-0 |page=61 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Nelson |first1=Gil |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9Ai2AwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Catalpa+bignonioides%22+%22fast%22&pg=PA166 |title=Trees of Eastern North America |last2=Earle |first2=Christopher J. |last3=Spellenberg |first3=Richard |date=2014-07-27 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1-4008-5299-4 |page=166 |language=en}}</ref> and widely grown as an [[ornamental tree]].{{fact|date=October 2023}} The catalpa has the distinction of bearing some of the showiest flowers of all the American native trees. Its value in this respect has long been recognized and it holds an assured place in the parks and gardens of all [[temperateness|temperate]] countries.<ref name=Keeler /> It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]],<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Catalpa bignonioides''|url=
https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/3201/Catalpa-bignonioides/Details | access-date=15 April 2020}}</ref> as has the gold-leafed [[cultivar]] ''C. bignonioides'' 'Aurea'.<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Catalpa bignonioides'' 'Aurea'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/93435/Catalpa-bignonioides-Aurea/Details | access-date=15 April 2020}}</ref> The purple-leaved hybrid [[Catalpa × erubescens|''Catalpa'' × ''erubescens'']] 'Purpurea' [[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''C. bignonioides'' 'Purpurea', has also achieved the award<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Catalpa'' × ''erubescens'' 'Purpurea'|url=
https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/98518/Catalpa-x-erubescens-Purpurea/Details | access-date=15 April 2020}}</ref> (confirmed 2017).<ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 16 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 24 January 2018}}</ref>

It prefers moist soil and full sun. It is easily raised from seeds which germinate early in the first season. It also multiplies readily from cuttings. The tree is fairly free from fungal diseases and has few insect enemies.<ref name=Keeler />

The wood is brittle and hard, but does not rot easily;{{fact|date=April 2024}} it is used for fence posts and railroad ties.

''Catalpa bignonioides'' contains varying levels of [[iridoid glycoside]]s that deter generalist herbivores, but which are tolerated by and concentrated in ''[[Ceratomia catalpae]]'' caterpillars.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Chemical Defense Across Three Trophic Levels: Catalpa bignonioides, the Caterpillar Ceratomia catalpae, and its Endoparasitoid Cotesia congregata|journal=Journal of Chemical Ecology|date=October 2011|volume=37|issue=10|pages=1063–70|doi=10.1007/s10886-011-0018-1|pmid=21948221|last1 = Lampert|first1 = Evan C.|last2=Dyer|first2=Lee A.|last3=Bowers|first3=M. Deane|bibcode=2011JCEco..37.1063L |s2cid=9937159}}</ref>  These caterpillars have a longstanding ecological relationship with the tree, and may defoliate a tree three or more times in a summer without killing it. Fishing enthusiasts prize the caterpillars as bait, particularly for catfish, and may freeze them for months after collecting them in the spring.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.motherearthnews.com/homesteading-and-livestock/catalpa-worms-zbcz1306.aspx|title=Leave Those Catalpa Worms Be|date=17 June 2013|author=Linda Holliday|publisher=Mother Earth News}}</ref>

It is one of two parents of the intergeneric hybrid tree [[× Chitalpa|× ''Chitalpa tashkentensis'']]. The other parent is ''[[Chilopsis linearis]]''. The cross was done by a Russian scientist in [[Tashkent]], [[Uzbekistan]]. The hybrid is sterile and at least two crosses exist, 'White Cloud' and 'Pink Dawn'.

==History==
The genus was common in Europe during the [[Tertiary period]]. In North America its [[fossil]] remains have been discovered in the [[miocene|Miocene rocks]] of the [[Yellowstone River]].<ref name=Keeler />
